echoes.note: The wilderness feeding of a great multitude with miraculous bread sets the controlling type that the chapter will name explicitly in v.31. High Volume and total Coherence with the manna economy (bread, gathering, leftovers, no waste); the feeding scene is the narrative enactment of the manna gift Jesus later interprets.

Philip's 'Where are we to buy bread... not sufficient' (v.7) closely mirrors Moses' despairing 'Where am I to get meat... shall flocks and herds be slaughtered to suffice them?' Strong structural and verbal Coherence: a leader confronted with an impossible crowd, mountain setting, and divine provision overriding human arithmetic.

Elisha multiplies twenty barley loaves to feed a hundred with leftovers, dismissing a servant's 'How can I set this before a hundred?' John alone specifies 'barley loaves' and 'what are these among so many?', and adds the leftovers motif. High Volume and verbal Recurrence make this the closest single OT analogue to the miracle's mechanics.

Asaph's 'he rained down manna... gave them grain of heaven... bread of the angels' is the psalm John will quote at v.31; its presence governs the feeding as the eschatological manna. High Coherence: the crowd reads the sign as a renewed wilderness banquet.

'He gave them bread from heaven in abundance' — a second psalmic celebration of the manna, reinforcing the satisfied-fullness motif ('when they were filled,' v.12). Lower distinctiveness than Ps 78 but adds Recurrence to the manna tradition active here.

The crowd's acclamation 'This is truly the prophet who comes into the world' (v.14) invokes the promised prophet-like-Moses. The Mosaic feeding miracle triggers a Mosaic-prophet expectation; high Coherence with John's prophet-and-king Christology.

John's editorial note 'Now the Passover was at hand' (v.4) frames the whole chapter under the paschal lamb, preparing the flesh-and-blood discourse (vv.51-56). Availability and Coherence are strong; the Passover anchor is authorial, though the feeding scene itself does not verbally cite Exodus 12.

Jesus 'went up into the mountain and sat there with his disciples' (v.3) before a meal faintly recalls Moses ascending Sinai where the elders 'beheld God and ate and drank.' Suggestive of a covenant-meal-on-the-mountain pattern but low Volume; contested.

The crowd's move to 'take him by force, to make him king' (v.15) faintly evokes Israel's improper demand for a king, which the LORD treats as rejection of his rule. Thematic rather than verbal; offered as a contested background to Jesus' refusal of a politicized kingship.

Jesus' 'It is I (ego eimi); do not be afraid' atop the storm reads, in John's idiom, as the divine self-naming 'I AM.' High Coherence with the chapter's later absolute 'I am' sayings; the theophanic-on-the-water setting elevates the otherwise ordinary phrase to divine self-disclosure.

'who alone... treads on the waves of the sea' ascribes sea-trampling to God alone. Jesus 'walking on the sea' enacts a prerogative the OT reserves for the Creator; strong Volume and Coherence with the I-AM disclosure that accompanies it.

'Your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters, yet your footprints were unseen' — a hymn of God's exodus march across the deep. Coheres with Jesus pathless on the water; the psalm's exodus frame fits John's Passover setting.

'Fear not... when you pass through the waters I will be with you' pairs the precise reassurance ('Don't be afraid') with passage through threatening waters. Coherence with the disciples' deliverance; the chapter's I-AM resonates with Isaiah 43:10 below.

'that you may... believe me and understand that I am he (ani hu / ego eimi)' supplies the LXX 'I am' that stands behind Jesus' words on the sea. Strengthens the case that v.20's ego eimi is theophanic rather than mere identification.

Seafarers in a wind-tossed storm cry out and God 'made the storm a calm' and 'brought them to their desired haven' — strikingly close to the boat reaching land 'immediately' (v.21). Good Coherence though John gives stilling-by-arrival rather than rebuke of the storm.

Under the Passover frame, a nighttime deliverance over/through the sea recalls the Red Sea crossing where Israel 'feared' then was saved. Typological rather than verbal; coheres with the exodus pattern saturating the chapter.

'He gave them bread out of heaven to eat' (v.31) is a formal citation ('as it is written') closest in wording to LXX Psalm 78:24 ('arton ouranou edoken autois'). The chapter's hermeneutical hinge; maximal Volume.

'I am about to rain bread from heaven for you' is the originating text behind the v.31 citation; Jesus directly contests its meaning ('it was not Moses who gave...'). The quotation conflates Exodus 16 with Psalm 78, so both are primary sources.

'You gave them bread from heaven for their hunger' is a third witness to the formula the crowd cites, showing the manna-from-heaven line was a fixed liturgical commonplace (Recurrence) rather than a single text.

'Why spend money for that which is not bread... eat what is good... that your soul may live' undergirds Jesus' contrast between 'food which perishes' and 'food which remains to eternal life' (v.27). Coherent invitation-to-true-nourishment background.

The manna that bred worms and stank when hoarded overnight gives concrete force to 'the food which perishes' (v.27). A plausible but faint verbal-conceptual link within the active manna matrix; contested as deliberate.

Wisdom's invitation 'Come, eat of my bread and drink of the wine I have mixed' stands behind 'I am the bread of life. He who comes to me will not hunger.' Strong Coherence: Jesus speaks as personified Wisdom hosting a banquet that confers life.

Wisdom says 'Come to me... those who eat me will hunger for more, those who drink me will thirst for more.' John inverts it ('will never hunger... never thirst'), a deliberate transformation signalling Jesus surpasses Wisdom/Torah. High Availability and Coherence; the inversion is the point.

'They shall not hunger or thirst... he who has pity will lead them' supplies the hunger-and-thirst-abolished promise of the eschatological return. Coheres tightly with v.35's double negation; an exilic-restoration backdrop to the bread of life.

The repeated 'I will raise him up at the last day' (vv.39-40) draws on the clearest OT resurrection text, 'many who sleep in the dust shall awake... to everlasting life.' Provides the Availability for John's last-day raising; recurs across the discourse.

'The Jews therefore murmured concerning him' (v.41,43) deliberately casts the audience as the wilderness generation that 'murmured against Moses and Aaron' over bread. High Volume and Coherence: the same verb-of-grumbling against the same gift (bread from heaven).

'It is written in the prophets, They will all be taught by God' (v.45) formally cites Isaiah 54:13 ('all your children shall be taught by the LORD'). A second explicit citation in the chapter; high Volume.

'They shall all know me, from the least to the greatest' (new-covenant interiority of divine teaching) reinforces the 'taught by God' citation and the drawing/learning that brings one to Jesus (vv.44-45). Strong Coherence as a secondary new-covenant source.

'Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died' (v.49) recalls the wilderness generation that craved, ate, and perished. The manna's described provision (Num 11:7-9) plus the death of that generation give Volume to Jesus' contrast with bread that lets one 'not die.'

'Not that anyone has seen the Father, except he who is from God' (v.46) reprises the Mosaic axiom 'no one shall see me and live.' Coheres with John's recurring claim that the Son alone has seen God (cf. 1:18); moderate Volume here.

'The bread which I will give for the life of the world is my flesh' (v.51), under the Passover frame, fuses bread with the slain paschal lamb whose flesh is eaten and whose blood saves. Typological Coherence prepares the eat-flesh scandal of the next pericope.

'Drink his blood' (v.53) collides head-on with the absolute Levitical prohibition: 'I will set my face against any who eats blood... the life is in the blood.' The scandal of vv.52-53 is unintelligible without this law; high Volume and Coherence as the offense John exploits.

'They shall eat the flesh that night' — the paschal lamb whose flesh is consumed. Jesus' demand to eat his flesh, set 'at Passover,' identifies him as the lamb; high typological Coherence binding the discourse to the chapter's opening note (v.4).

'You shall not eat flesh with its life, that is, its blood' is the primal Noachic blood prohibition predating Sinai, broadening the scandal of v.53 beyond Israel to a universal taboo. Adds Recurrence to the blood-prohibition background.

'Only be sure that you do not eat the blood, for the blood is the life' restates the prohibition with the life-in-the-blood rationale that John ironically affirms (the blood gives life). Reinforces the contested commandment behind the discourse.

Wisdom's 'those who eat me... those who drink me' returns here with literal eating and drinking, deepening the Wisdom-banquet identification of Jesus. Coheres with v.35; the eat/drink pairing strengthens the Sirach link.

'Eat of my bread and drink of the wine I have mixed' — Wisdom's bread-and-wine banquet underlies the flesh-as-food/blood-as-drink doubling of vv.53-56. Lower distinctiveness than the Leviticus collision but adds the sapiential meal frame.

'Not as our fathers ate the manna, and died' (v.58) closes the discourse by again invoking the heaven-bread of Exodus 16, now surpassed. Recurrence of the governing manna text rather than a fresh allusion.

'What if you would see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?' (v.62) trades on the Danielic Son of Man who comes with the clouds before the Ancient of Days; John reverses the vector to ascent. Provides the title's apocalyptic Availability.

'It is the spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing' (v.63) echoes the valley-of-bones promise 'I will put my spirit within you, and you shall live.' Coherent spirit-gives-life theology; the dry-bones spirit animates dead flesh.

'The Egyptians are flesh and not spirit' supplies the flesh/spirit antithesis behind 'the flesh profits nothing' (v.63), where flesh is the weak human plane and spirit the divine. Conceptual Coherence; moderate Volume.

'The spirit who gives life' (v.63) may glance at the breath of life by which the LORD made the man a living being. Foundational but diffuse; offered as a faint creational backdrop to life-giving Spirit.

Peter's 'you are the Holy One of God' (v.69) resonates with 'you will not let your Holy One see corruption,' a key resurrection/messianic title. Coheres with the chapter's raising-on-the-last-day refrain; the holy-one designation is OT-rooted.

Aaron is 'the holy one of the LORD' — the only OT figure given nearly this exact title, offering a priestly alternative background to Peter's confession (v.69). Lower Volume than Psalm 16; contested as the operative source.
'You have the words of eternal life' (v.68) faintly recalls Moses' 'it is no empty word for you, but your very life.' The word-as-life motif suits John's Mosaic typology; diffuse and contested.
